query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A machine-learning model that integrates high-throughput first-principles phonon calculations with experimental lattice thermal conductivity measurements can accurately predict low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys by learning disorder‐sensitive descriptors (such as mass variance, bond stiffness fluctuation, and local lattice distortion), outperforming conventional predictive approaches.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys composed of multiple principal elements with inherent chemical disorder and complex atomic arrangements.
generation.intervention: Develop and train a data-driven model using both simulated phonon data and validated experimental thermal conductivity measurements.
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted over a temperature range from near room temperature to high-temperature operational conditions in single-phase, disordered HEAs without significant phase separation or additional microstructural complexities.
generation.structural_mediator: Descriptors capturing mass variance, bond stiffness fluctuations, and local lattice distortions arising from chemical disorder.
generation.mechanism: The model leverages disorder-sensitive descriptors to quantify the enhanced phonon scattering (leading to shorter phonon lifetimes) due to atomic-scale mass and bonding fluctuations, thereby predicting lower phonon thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The machine-learning approach will deliver predictions with statistically significant reduced error margins relative to conventional ab initio or phenomenological models when compared against time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) measurements of lattice thermal conductivity.
generation.baseline: Current predictive methods that do not fully capture the disorder-induced phonon scattering in HEAs, resulting in higher prediction errors.
generation.boundary: This approach is applicable primarily to chemically disordered, single-phase HEAs operating within the experimentally validated temperature range; predictions may not hold for alloys with phase instabilities or additional engineered microstructural features (e.g., deliberate porosity).
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement over existing methods remains uncertain until extensive benchmarking is performed, and variability in experimental data may affect model training.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a set of HEA compositions predicted by the ML model to exhibit low lattice thermal conductivity. Synthesize these alloys and perform time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) measurements over the target temperature range.
measurements: Phonon lifetime (via indirect phonon dispersion analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally measured lattice thermal conductivities consistently deviate from the model predictions beyond the defined preset confidence interval (i.e., prediction error exceeds a predetermined threshold), then the hypothesis that the ML model reliably predicts low phonon thermal conductivity in HEAs will be falsified.

Existing data-driven approaches for exploring high-entropy alloys (HEAs) face three challenges: numerous element-combination candidates, designing appropriate descriptors, and limited and biased existing data. To overcome these issues, here we show the development of an evidence-based material recommender system (ERS) that adopts Dempster–Shafer theory, a general framework for reasoning with uncertainty. Herein, without using material descriptors, we model, collect and combine pieces of evidence from data about the HEA phase existence of alloys. To evaluate the ERS, we compared its HEA-recommendation capability with those of matrix-factorization- and supervised-learning-based recommender systems on four widely known datasets of up-to-five-component alloys. The k-fold cross-validation on the datasets suggests that the ERS outperforms all competitors. Furthermore, the ERS shows good extrapolation capabilities in recommending quaternary and quinary HEAs. We experimentally validated the most strongly recommended Fe–Co-based magnetic HEA (namely, FeCoMnNi) and confirmed that its thin film shows a body-centered cubic structure. cited_evidence.kind: web:Conductive and wear performance of the NbMoTaW coatings on AFM probe tips
cited_evidence.text: In summary, this study has established a conductivity model for the HEA system Nb-Mo-Ta-W, designed alloy compositions with high conductivity and wear resistance, which can be applied to enhance the atomic-level resolution and lifespan of atomic force microscope probes. By adjusting the composition, a refractory high-entropy material of Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 was endowed with both high hardness and electrical conductivity. We indicate that the conductivity of Nb-Mo-Ta-W HEAs can be modulated through the cocktail effect but tends to differ by an order of magnitude compared to linear combinations. The reasons for the decrease in conductivity are attributed to changes in the plasma frequency and relaxation time resulting from lattice distortions, alterations in the effective mass and density of free electrons, and variations in the crystalline size after the formation of HEAs.

cited_evidence.kind: web:Tailoring local chemical fluctuation and lattice thermal conductivity
cited_evidence.text: The difference in electronegativity (another intrinsic characteristic of element) affects the local chemical bonding and plays a vital role for the properties of high-entropy materials, such as the strength and ductility of high-entropy alloys (, , ) for engineered applications, the charge redistribution of high-entropy catalysts () for hydrogen evolution reaction, and the electron transport of high-entropy oxides () for lithium-ion battery. Similar to the mass and strain field fluctuations, the electronegativity difference could increase the complexity of chemical bonding between atoms as the chemical bond fluctuation. Therefore, the contribution of electronegativity difference was also included into the Callaway-Debye model for lattice thermal conductivity calculation (Supplementary Text and table S6). We have found that the chemical bond fluctuation (ΓC) demonstrates a noticeable contribution to lattice thermal conductivity in GeTe-AgSbMn compared to other two samples (Fig. 5B), which is derived from the decreased electronegativity difference of Mn (1.55), Pb (2.33), and Sn (1.96) to other constituent elements Ge (2.01), Ag (1.93), Sb (2.05), and Te (2.10).

AbstractThe ability to predict and understand phases in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) is still being debated, and primarily true predictive capabilities derive from the known thermodynamics of materials. The present work demonstrates that prior work using high-throughput first-principles calculations may be further utilized to provide direct insight into the temperature- and composition-dependent phase evolution in HEAs, particularly Al-containing HEAs with a strengthening multiphase microstructure. Using a simple model with parameters derived from first-principles calculations, we reproduce the major features associated with Al-containing phases, demonstrating a generalizable approach for exploring potential phase evolution where little experimental data exists. Neutron scattering, in situ microscopy, and calorimetry measurements suggest that our high-throughput Monte Carlo technique captures both qualitative and quantitative features for both intermetallic phase formation and microstructure evolution at lower temperatures. Each of these approaches has its own strengths and weaknesses. For example, ab initio and MD are very time-consuming and can hardly be used to predict structures of the alloys in a high-throughput manner. Phenomenological rules are based on empirical observations and are easy for calculations, but the accuracy of their predictions does not exceed 72% []. CALPHAD modeling can be quite throughput, however it requires significant computing resources. In addition, the accuracy of the CALPHAD predictions can be limited due to the absence of a reliable database for HEAs []. The machine learning approach is sensitive to the size and composition of a training dataset, but the prediction accuracy of this method can attain more than 90% []. frame.goal: To reliably predict low phonon thermal conductivity in HEAs and thereby guide material selection or design for improved thermal insulation.
frame.limitation: No clearly defined and testable predictive approach currently exists to systematically and accurately identify HEAs with exceptionally low phonon thermal conductivity.

It must include a rationale describing why the model correctly captures phonon behavior in high-entropy alloys.
It must define the range of compositions or structures for which the model is valid.

decision.trend: Beginning in late 2022, a lattice-dynamics study (PMC9726824) showed that the random solution nature of high-entropy alloys strongly suppresses phonon lifetimes and lowers thermal conductivity. Shortly after, a DFT-based approach (PMC9822225) used advanced simulations to confirm significantly reduced phonon conductivity in a high-entropy thermoelectric system, yet it relied on specific chemical compositions without providing a widely applicable predictive framework. Most recently, an experimental demonstration of porous high-entropy ceramics (PMC10143762) highlighted that even lower thermal conductivities can be achieved via engineered porosity, but no unified methodology exists to systematically identify low-phonon-conductivity compositions across the broad HEA compositional space.
decision.unsolved: While individual experiments and computational case studies have validated low phonon thermal conductivity for particular high-entropy systems, there remains no robust, broadly validated approach to predict such behavior across diverse multi-element compositions with complex atomic disorder. Methods combining advanced simulation and data analysis are still needed to guide and verify these predictions at scale.
decision.lever: Build and train a machine-learning model that integrates high-throughput first-principles phonon calculations and experimental data to learn disorder-sensitive descriptors—encompassing mass variance, bond stiffness fluctuation, and local environment distortions—for a wide range of compositionally complex HEAs. Use these descriptors to predict the lattice thermal conductivity over the entire composition space and validate predictions via direct high-temperature thermal conductivity measurements (e.g., time-domain thermoreflectance). A deviation between predicted and measured conductivities beyond a preset confidence interval would falsify the hypothesis.
decision.why: This approach combines growing evidence on the role of chemical disorder in phonon scattering with modern data-driven strategies. It systematically addresses challenges identified in prior works and can be decisively tested with well-defined thermal conductivity experiments for targeted HEA compositions.
